REP: Thanks for making time before the lunch rush, Alan. I'd like to spend about fifteen minutes on how you handle sick visits today, and then, if it makes sense, show you how RapidPanel works. Does that work for you?
CUSTOMER: Sure. Fifteen minutes is about what I've got before the phones go crazy. Monday mornings are all the weekend refills and the faxes from the clinics.
REP: When a parent walks in with a kid who has a sore throat, what usually happens today?
CUSTOMER: Honestly, we point them to the throat lozenges and the children's ibuprofen, and if it looks like more than a cold we send them to the urgent care across the highway. Then they sit there for two hours, and half the time they come back here at six o'clock asking if we can fill an antibiotic before we close.
REP: How often does that happen in a typical week this time of year?
CUSTOMER: September, maybe ten a week. Once flu season hits in January it's double that, easily. Some days it feels like every other customer is coughing. And it's not just kids. We get a lot of teachers from the middle school down the road, and they can't take a whole afternoon off to sit in urgent care.
REP: And when they go to urgent care, what does that cost you?
CUSTOMER: More than people think. The urgent care has a chain pharmacy right in the same plaza, so a lot of those prescriptions never come back to us. And once a family moves their kids' prescriptions, the parents' maintenance meds tend to follow. I've lost whole households that way.
REP: What would it mean for you if you could run that test right here and hand them a result in about ten minutes?
CUSTOMER: I'd keep the fill, I'd sell the OTC products that go with it, and frankly it's good for our reputation. People would see us as the place that actually helps, not the place that sends you somewhere else. We've been here thirty-one years. My dad opened this store, and the whole reason people pick us over the chains is that we know them by name. Every time I send someone across the highway, it feels like I'm giving that away.
REP: That's exactly what RapidPanel is built for. Strep, flu and COVID run on one small reader, results come back in about ten minutes, and we train your team and work through the CLIA waiver paperwork with you.
CUSTOMER: It sounds good, but I'm worried about the time. On Saturdays it's just me and one tech, and we're already slammed.
REP: That's a fair worry, and Saturdays are exactly when the sick kids show up. What does a Saturday look like for you, hour by hour?
CUSTOMER: Nine to one is brutal. We're doing twenty scripts an hour and the drive-through never stops. After one o'clock it falls off a cliff. My tech mostly restocks and I catch up on calls and prior authorizations. Honestly, some Saturday afternoons I'm looking for things to do.
REP: Then that afternoon is your window. The swab takes your tech about two minutes, the reader runs on its own, and you spend about three minutes on the result and the note. Most of our independents only take test appointments after 1 p.m. on Saturdays, booked through a QR code on the window. Would afternoon-only testing work for you?
CUSTOMER: Afternoon-only, yeah. I could live with that. Denise would probably like having something to do besides restocking, to be honest.
REP: Good. What else would need to be true for this to make sense for Brookside?
CUSTOMER: The numbers have to work. The last vendor who pitched me testing wanted so much per kit that I'd have needed forty tests a month just to break even. I'm not going to see forty a month in this neighborhood, not outside of January anyway. And I'm not going to push tests on people who don't need them just to hit a number.
REP: Break-even is the right way to look at it. Roughly how many of those ten weekly sore-throat customers do you think would pay cash for a test?
CUSTOMER: If it's under forty dollars? Maybe half of them. Parents will pay to skip a two-hour wait. The ones with high-deductible plans would pay it without blinking, because urgent care costs them more than that before they even see anyone.
REP: Then here's the math. Each test costs you about twelve dollars, and most independents charge thirty-five to forty, so you keep over twenty dollars a test before the fill. At five tests a week you've paid off the first two-box order in about three weeks. The reader is on loan, so there's no equipment cost, and if kits get within ninety days of expiry we swap them once a year. Does that change the picture?
CUSTOMER: That's a lot better than what I saw last time. Okay. If I'm clearing twenty dollars a test and keeping the prescription, that's a different conversation.
REP: Who else should be part of the decision?
CUSTOMER: My wife does the books, so she'll want to see the agreement. She reads every line of every contract, so send her the real one, not a brochure. And Denise, my lead tech, would be the one doing the swabs.
REP: Makes sense. Here's what I'd suggest. I'll email you and your wife the agreement and the break-even sheet today, and I'll come back Thursday the 17th at 2 p.m. to walk you and Denise through the CLIA packet and the training plan. Does that time work?
CUSTOMER: Thursday at two works. I'll make sure Denise is on.
REP: Perfect. Agreement and break-even sheet in your inbox by end of day, and I'll see you and Denise on Thursday the 17th at two.
CUSTOMER: Sounds good. Thanks, Maya.
